title: Second Judge Bars Trump's Appeal, Citing Low Chances of Court Success – NPR Report
body:
A federal judge in Virginia has moved to halt the construction of a privately funded “triumphal arch” that former President Donald Trump plans to erect on the National Mall, issuing a preliminary injunction that could keep the structure off the iconic landscape indefinitely. The decision, announced by U.S. District Judge Leonie Brinkema on Friday, follows a similar ruling by a Washington, D.C., judge earlier this week that temporarily blocked the project. Brinkema’s order signals a growing judicial skepticism that the monument, billed as a celebration of “America’s greatness,” can survive legal scrutiny.

The Virginia case centers on the National Park Service’s longstanding authority to regulate the use of federal lands, a power that has been repeatedly upheld by courts when private entities seek to place structures on the Mall. Prosecutors for the National Park Service argue that the arch violates the 1906 “Commemorative Works Act,” which restricts new monuments and memorials in the Mall’s core unless Congress explicitly authorizes them. Trump’s team counters that the arch is a temporary, privately financed installation that does not require federal approval, citing a 2021 executive order that purportedly expands private rights to display patriotic symbols on public property.

Judge Brinkema, who has presided over high‑profile cases involving political figures, said during the hearing that the government’s arguments “appear substantially stronger” and that the arch is “unlikely to succeed on the merits” if the case proceeds to trial. She noted that the National Park Service had already denied the permit application, citing concerns about the arch’s size, location, and potential to disrupt the Mall’s historic vista. The judge’s preliminary injunction will freeze any further work on the structure pending a full trial, effectively pausing a project that has already drawn intense public and media attention.

Legal experts see the Virginia ruling as a critical test of the limits of private monuments on federal ground. Professor Emily Rosenberg of Georgetown Law points out that the “Commemorative Works Act” was designed to protect the Mall’s symbolic integrity, and that recent attempts to bypass it could set a precedent for future private installations. “If the courts allow a privately funded arch to stand without congressional authorization, it could open the floodgates for a host of partisan monuments that would fundamentally alter the character of the nation’s most hallowed public space,” she warned.

Political reactions have been sharply divided. Supporters of the former president argue that the injunction represents an overreach by a liberal‑leaning judiciary intent on silencing dissenting voices. They claim the arch is a lawful expression of patriotism that should not be subject to bureaucratic gatekeeping. Conversely, preservationists and many lawmakers stress the need to maintain the Mall’s historic openness and warn that allowing the arch could undermine the careful planning that has shaped the capital’s visual narrative for over a century.

The case now moves toward a full trial, where both sides will present detailed evidence on the legal and historical merits of the proposed structure. The National Park Service is expected to continue defending its regulatory authority, while Trump’s legal team is likely to appeal any adverse rulings and may seek a legislative solution to secure the arch’s future. The outcome will not only determine the fate of this particular monument but could also influence how future private commemorations are treated on federal land.

As the nation watches, the pending litigation underscores a broader debate over who gets to decide what symbols occupy America’s most public spaces. Whether the arch will ever rise on the Mall remains uncertain, but the courts are poised to play a decisive role in defining the boundaries between private initiative and public stewardship in the capital’s historic heart.
